newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TELECOMS-Telstra sale seen struggling in Senate.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TELECOMS-Telstra sale seen struggling in Senate.

text.p: The Australian government's plans to sell a third of Telstra Corp are likely to remain hostage to a hostile Senate for the rest of this year and possibly well into next year, political analysts say.
The Telstra sale bill is currently waiting to be debated in the Senate by October 28 at the earliest.

The Liberal-National government needs two votes of the Senate's 10 balance-of-power senators to get the legislation through. The key to passing the Telstra bill is held by two Independents, Brian Harradine and Mal Colston, who have not said which way they will vote.
All other non-government senators, including the opposition Labor, Democrat and Greens parties have indicated they will oppose the bill.
Political analyst Malcolm Mackerras said the bill would be rejected this year but passed next year.
"My hunch is it will become law about April next year," Mackerras told Reuters on Thursday.
Mackerras said Colston would vote for and Harradine would vote against it this year and therefore it would fail to pass.
"Next year, after the government has waited the necessary three months under section 57 of the constitution, it will be presented again and passed a second time."
Mackerras predicted that Harradine would decide belatedly that the government had a mandate for it and it would then pass.
"It seems to me that everything Colston has ever said indicates that he believes in the mandate theory, and would therefore vote for the bill."
"I will be surprised if the Telstra bill is not the law of the land in May next year," he said.
Other commentators said it would be difficult to predict the fate of the bill in the Senate.
"It's very hard to guess which way it will go," said Scott Bennett, a lecturer in politial science at the Australian National University.

Harradine has previously said he would not back the bill in its present form. He suggested the government issue redeemable preference shares in Telstra, but Treasurer Peter Costello said this "held no attraction".

"It essentially would be borrowing off back of the Telstra security and if the government is to borrow it would prefer to borrow on its own account with its own credit rating," Costello told parliament.
Colston, a Labor defector, has said he was "favourably disposed" to the partial privatisation of Telstra, but there were a few things he'd "like to talk to the government about".
The government has said it is quite happy to talk.
The Telstra bill was passed in the lower house, the House of Representatives, on May 9 and sent to the Senate the same day.
It was was referred to a Senate inquiry on May 21.

The inquiry, dominated by non-government parties, on September 9 recommended against the sale, finding no substantial evidence to back the government's claim the economy and consumers would benefit from the sale.
The government said in its August budget it saw proceeds from the Telstra sale in 1997/98 and 1998/99. The sale will raise an estimated $8 billion.
